# Phase 2 — Discourse Report: "Politics Has Five Questions" (v1)

- **Reviewer:** Phase 2 editor (discourse mapping and originality audit)
- **Date:** 2026-07-30/31
- **Method:** Every work discussed below was fetched and read this session (at the depth stated in the matching source note under `agents/editor/research/sources/`). Where access was abstract-level or search-summary-level, that is said explicitly. Nothing is cited from memory alone.

---

## 1. Predecessors and neighbors

The draft enters a field that is far more crowded than its reference list suggests. Its ten footnotes are all academic or data-infrastructural; its actual nearest neighbors — a two-decade tradition of popular multi-axis taxonomies and a 2023 trade book making the identical opening move — go unmentioned. Map:

### 1a. The popular multi-axis tradition (uncited; nearest in content)

**Nolan chart / Political Compass (2 axes).** The Political Compass ([politicalcompass.org/analysis2](https://www.politicalcompass.org/analysis2)) has argued since 2001, on the Nolan chart's 1969 template, that the left-right line is "certainly fine for discussing economics but... wrongly used to describe social attitudes," with a reductio the draft could have written: "the further left a country sits, the more socially liberal its attitudes are. On that basis, North Korea must be a shining model of human rights and social freedoms!" Its stock illustrations include France's National Rally — "far right" with economics "sometimes to the left of even the French Socialist Party" — which is the draft's welfare-nationalist demonstration avant la lettre. The draft's founding gesture (the spectrum is a conflation of separable disagreements) is the founding gesture of this entire genre.

**8values (4 axes).** This is the decisive neighbor. The open-source 8values test ([8values.github.io](https://8values.github.io/); [repo](https://github.com/8values/8values.github.io)) measures: **Economic: Equality ↔ Markets; Civil: Liberty ↔ Authority; Societal: Tradition ↔ Progress; Diplomatic: Nation ↔ Globe**. Three of the draft's five axes carry *verbatim* the same pole names (Equality↔Markets, Liberty↔Authority, Progress↔Tradition), and the fourth (Belonging: Universal↔Communal) is a philosophically upgraded cousin of Nation↔Globe (the draft's version is genuinely better: it separates scope-of-obligation from foreign-policy posture, which it exports to a module — 8values conflates them). 8values even contains a crude ancestor of the draft's central architectural move: after scoring your four coordinates it names your "Closest Match" ideology, i.e., coordinates first, nearest named family second — though 8values treats the naming step as an embarrassment ("much less accurate than the values and axes") where the draft builds a disciplined semantics for it. Whatever the causal history, the surface identity is total enough that any reader who has seen 8values will assume derivation. The draft must either cite it and differentiate, or be pattern-matched to it involuntarily.

**9Axes and PolitiScales (8–9 axes).** The axis-proliferating successors show that even the draft's *periphery* is pre-explored. 9Axes ([9axes.github.io](https://9axes.github.io/)) adds Federal↔Unitary (≈ the draft's centralization tag), Democratic↔Authoritarian (≈ the regime-type tag), Militarist↔Pacifist (≈ the Restraint↔Intervention module), Secular↔Religious (≈ the basis-of-belonging tag). PolitiScales ([politiscales.party/about](https://politiscales.party/about)) has an Ecology↔Production axis (≈ Growth↔Ecology module) and a Revolution↔Reform axis (a cousin of Insurgent↔Institutional framed as method-of-change). These tests also model the failure the draft warns against — undisciplined axis multiplication with no salience, naming, or usage rules — and are therefore useful to the draft as a foil, not only a liability.

**Arnold Kling, *The Three Languages of Politics*.** Read via [Quillette's review](https://quillette.com/2018/08/08/the-three-languages-of-politics-a-review/). Kling's three axes (oppressor↔oppressed, civilization↔barbarism, liberty↔coercion) are *rhetorical heuristics of three American tribes*, not positional coordinates — a different project. But the draft's closing formula ("We do not need a more complicated compass. We need a grammar") and especially its §XI.7 charitable-poles table (each pole = a good pursued and a failure feared) are Klingian moves: Kling's whole method is steelmanning each language so that "treating people who use other heuristics as reasonable" becomes possible. The grammar framing is not novel; the draft's *positional* grammar is distinct from Kling's *rhetorical* one, and one clause could both credit and differentiate.

### 1b. The academic multidimensionality literature (partially cited)

**Hooghe–Marks GAL/TAN.** Read the original paper ([Hooghe, Marks & Wilson 2002, PDF](https://garymarks.web.unc.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/13018/2016/09/hooghe-marks-wilson-does-leftright-structure-party-positions-on-European-integration.pdf)): the "new politics" dimension runs **green/alternative/libertarian ↔ traditionalism/authority/nationalism**, conceptually independent of economic left-right, with TAN the strongest predictor of Euroscepticism. This matters acutely: TAN bundles precisely the draft's Tradition + Authority + Communal poles, and the Chapel Hill Expert Survey — the draft's own data source — was built around this two-dimensional framework. So when the draft's §II composites find Culture, Coercion, and Belonging correlating at .78–.82, it has substantially *rediscovered the design dimension of its own dataset* and presented it as a framework-confirming empirical pattern. Without a GAL/TAN citation, a political scientist reads §II as naive; with one, the same result becomes an honest and interesting claim ("the reigning two-dimensional model welds together three questions that current politics is visibly unwelding — Milei is the proof").

**Kitschelt's diagonal; Eysenck; Inglehart–Norris** (search-summary level; see `two-dimensional-precursors` note). Eysenck (1954) found two psychometric dimensions (Radicalism and tough-/tender-mindedness — Stalinists and Nazis alike tough-minded) seventy years ago. Kitschelt (1994) showed postindustrial party competition runs along a left-libertarian ↔ right-authoritarian *diagonal* in the 2D space — which is exactly why the draft's CHES composites correlate: European parties occupy the diagonal. Inglehart–Norris's *Cultural Backlash* treats authoritarian populism as a cultural-dimension backlash distinct from economics. None cited; Kitschelt in particular is the standard explanation for the empirical bundling the draft describes as "history is powerful enough to bind their answers together."

**Bobbio, *Left and Right*** (search-summary/encyclopedic level; see note). The canonical *substantive* defense of the single dimension: left and right are real and enduringly divided by attitudes to equality — a "horizontal or egalitarian conception of society" versus a "vertical or inegalitarian" one. For a philosophy venue this is the most conspicuous scholarly absence, because it is the strongest published claim that the draft's five questions are five theaters of one war (equality applied to wealth, coercion, culture, membership, and elites). The draft's §VIII engages only the *coordination* defense of left-right, never the *substantive* one. Christian Gonzalez's reply to Hyrum Lewis ([Heterodox Academy](https://heterodoxacademy.org/blog/the-political-spectrum-does-exist-a-reply-to-hyrum-lewis/)) makes the same egalitarianism-based defense in blog form: "the left advances a politics of egalitarianism, while the right opposes the left and attempts to defend some other value."

**Converse 1964** (full PDF read: [purdue-hosted copy](https://web.ics.purdue.edu/~hoganr/Soc%20312/The%20nature%20of%20belief%20systems%20in%20mass%20publics%201964.pdf)). Mass publics show little ideological constraint; only a few percent genuinely use liberal-conservative abstractions; panel data reveal "non-attitudes." Directly relevant to whether a *public* five-axis vocabulary describes anything ordinary citizens could use. Uncited.

**Poole–Rosenthal** ([voteview.com/about](https://voteview.com/about)). "The primary dimension through most of American history has been 'liberal' vs. 'conservative'," with a second dimension absorbing cross-cutting issues. The statistical-parsimony objection to five coordinates. Uncited.

### 1c. The nearest popular predecessor and standing counterargument: Lewis & Lewis

*The Myth of Left and Right* (Hyrum & Verlan Lewis, OUP 2023) was read via two reviews ([Baylor, Medium](https://medium.com/@cbaylor/reviewing-the-myth-of-left-and-right-by-hyrum-and-verlan-lewis-5644a509999d); [Trepanier, Kirk Center](https://kirkcenter.org/reviews/essentially-lying-about-the-left-and-right/)), Hyrum Lewis's own essay ([Quillette 2017](https://quillette.com/2017/05/03/time-retire-political-spectrum/)), and the Caplan–Lewis exchange ([betonit.ai](https://www.betonit.ai/p/the-myth-of-left-and-right-the-last)). Their claim: there is no essence uniting left or right; "people adopt the positions of a tribe first and only then invent a story that ties all those positions together"; ideologies are "reverse engineered to fit tribal actions and attachments." This is the draft's §VIII ("left and right are coalition names... the bundles move") published three years earlier as a book — *and* it cuts against the draft, because the Lewises resist small-n dimensional replacements too. In the Caplan exchange, Lewis is explicit: the problem is that "there is more than one issue in politics" — politics is like biology (many species) or chemistry (many elements) — so the remedy is unbundling into *issues*, not re-bundling into five axes: "why not just say 'anti-market' instead of 'left-wing'?" The draft's position is a genuine third way between Caplan's pragmatic monism and Lewis's eliminativism, but v1 never names either, and so never claims the ground it actually occupies.

### 1d. The populism-decomposition literature (half cited)

The draft cites Mudde and Caramani and characterizes both accurately (see §4 below). What it does not cite:

- **Müller, *What Is Populism?*** (read via [LSE review](https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/lsereviewofbooks/2016/12/14/book-review-what-is-populism-by-jan-werner-muller/) with corroborating search results): the criterion of populism is anti-pluralism — populists "claim that they, and they alone, represent the people," a moral monopoly of representation. The draft's "moral dualism," "unitarism," and pluralism facet ("are opposition and competing interests permanently legitimate?") are Müller's apparatus in all but name. This is the clearest single attribution gap in the piece, and the riskiest, because Müller's is the best-known trade book on the subject among the draft's likely readers.
- **Akkerman, Mudde & Zaslove 2014** ([CPS](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0010414013512600), abstract/repository level): the standard populist-attitudes battery already decomposes populism into anti-elitism, people-centrism, and Manicheism, measured separately from *pluralist* and *elitist* attitudes. The draft's four facets (anti-establishment ≈ anti-elitism; directism ≈ people-centrism; pluralism ≈ the pluralism scale; legitimation ≈ Caramani's will/reason plus the elitism scale) reinvent this measurement scheme at the conceptual level.
- **POPPA** ([poppa-data.eu](https://poppa-data.eu/)): party-level expert measurement of populism's sub-attributes plus style, organization, and democratic commitment, 312 parties in 31 countries. Disaggregated populism scoring is existing infrastructure, not a proposal.
- **Uscinski et al. 2021** ([abstract](https://scholarship.miami.edu/esploro/outputs/journalArticle/American-Politics-in-Two-Dimensions-Partisan/991031660574802976)) *is* cited, accurately, and is the best empirical warrant for the System axis being real and orthogonal. One caveat the draft elides: Uscinski et al.'s anti-establishment dimension is partly a psychological syndrome (conspiracy thinking, antisocial traits, violence acceptance), which sits awkwardly under the draft's charitable Insurgent pole ("responsiveness and renewal").

### 1e. Prior "coordinates before categories" essays

Searched for prior essays proposing five-or-more-axis political vocabularies with a coordinates-then-names architecture (queries across "five axes/five dimensions political spectrum," taxonomy-proposal phrasing, SSC/LessWrong-adjacent material). Found: the test tradition above; an 8values-adjacent explainer on "multidimensional political coordinates" at 8values.cc (403 on fetch — could not read; noting per protocol); and, in the rationalist-adjacent space, the dominant artifacts are *one-dimension* theories (Scott Alexander's [Thrive/Survive](https://slatestarcodex.com/2013/03/04/a-thrivesurvive-theory-of-the-political-spectrum/), which answers "why do unrelated positions cluster?" with a single generative variable, while conceding "once an issue is associated with one side or the other, the association is self-perpetuating"). I found **no prior essay that combines (a) five-plus named axes, (b) a prototype-family lexicon with modifiers, and (c) explicit usage rules (metadata, no-master-score, evidence hierarchy)**. The *components* are all pre-existing; the assembled *manual* is not. Also noted for the record: the "prototype, not checklist" semantics itself is thirty years old in political science — Collier & Mahon 1993 on family-resemblance and radial categories ([APSR](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-political-science-review/article/abs/conceptual-stretching-revisited-adapting-categories-in-comparative-analysis/52A5DA1F2B8A9516A45C04F5B165E1C5), abstract level) — and the draft's "Welfare Nationalist" family renames "welfare chauvinism," coined by Andersen & Bjørklund in 1990 and the subject of thirty years of research ([ECPS vocabulary entry](https://www.populismstudies.org/Vocabulary/welfare-chauvinism/); [Careja & Harris 2022](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/09589287211068796), search-summary level).

---

## 2. Originality verdict

**Classification: novel synthesis with two significant unwitting reinventions, currently packaged in a way that overstates its novelty by omission.**

Element by element:

**Reinvented (must be acknowledged):**
1. **The four non-System axes ≈ 8values' four axes**, two/three with verbatim pole names. Whether convergent or derived, the identity is public and checkable. (Reported against interest: the draft's Belonging axis is a real improvement over 8values' Diplomatic axis, and the draft's decision to push foreign policy into a module is exactly the fix 8values needed. The improvement is only visible if the predecessor is named.)
2. **The four System facets ≈ the existing populism-measurement scheme** (Akkerman et al.'s anti-elitism/people-centrism/Manicheism + pluralism scale; Müller's anti-pluralism; Caramani's legitimation contrast; POPPA/CHES party measures). Caramani and Mudde are cited; Müller and the measurement literature are not.
3. Smaller reinventions: "Welfare Nationalist" ≈ welfare chauvinism (1990); prototype-family semantics ≈ Collier & Mahon's radial categories (1993); the culture+coercion+belonging bundle ≈ GAL/TAN (2002); "left/right as tribal coalition names" ≈ Lewis & Lewis (2017/2023); the compression critique itself ≈ the Nolan/Political Compass genre (1969–).

**Genuinely novel (defensible as such):**
1. **The two-function separation as an explicit design principle** — coordinates describe positions, family names identify neighborhoods, and ordinary labels fail because they are forced to do both at once. Nothing I could find states this. 8values' "Closest Match" stumbles into the structure but treats the naming layer as noise; the draft is the first to give it a semantics. This is the piece's real thesis and its strongest claim to originality.
2. **The rules-of-use layer**: salience/confidence/time/object metadata; rhetoric/program/practice profiles; the no-master-score rule with decomposable distance; the evidence hierarchy; the one-modifier rule; dated profiles. No predecessor — popular or academic — offers a *usage discipline* for a public vocabulary. (CHES records position/salience/dissent/blurring separately, and the draft credits it; extending that practice to ordinary political speech is new.)
3. **The hierarchical System axis** — a deliberately approximate public gloss (Populist↔Establishment) formally subordinated to rigorous facets, with the three-way disambiguation of populist (substantive) / establishment (contextual) / institutional (preferential). The facets are borrowed; the two-level public/analytic architecture and the disambiguation are not, and the §IV linguistic distinctions are the best pages in the essay.
4. **The retention thesis**: left/right kept *above* the coordinates as coalition names — a constructive third position between Caplan's "the spectrum is useful, keep it" and Lewis's "it's a delusion, abolish it." Novel as a positioning, but only if the flanking positions are named; unclaimed territory is invisible.

**Where the piece would be strengthened by citing work it ignores:** 8values (one sentence of genealogy defuses the deadliest pattern-match); Lewis & Lewis (converts the strongest counterargument into the essay's dialectical frame); Müller (§IV); GAL/TAN + Kitschelt (§II — turns an apparent naivety into a pointed claim); Bobbio (§VIII — the substantive defense it currently ducks); welfare chauvinism (§VI); Kling (§XI.7/§XIII); Collier & Mahon (§VI, optional). **Where it claims novelty it lacks:** mostly by implication rather than assertion — the essay never says "no one has done this," but by citing only academic anchors and no neighbors it *performs* a novelty it does not have at the axis level. The one explicit overreach: §II's "This is exactly what the framework should predict" presents the GAL/TAN bundle as a framework result.

---

## 3. The strongest existing counterargument

**Ranking:** (a) Lewis-style anti-essentialism/granularity > (c) dimensional parsimony > (b) Converse > (d) coordination defense.

**(d) Coordination defenses** (Caplan: "the spectrum helps us to understand political identity and political conflict. Which it totally does") are adequately handled — §VIII is a fair and even elegant concession, and the draft's "file name vs contents" division of labor is a real answer. What §VIII does *not* handle is the **substantive** defense (Bobbio/Gonzalez: the line tracks a real attitude toward equality). That defense deserves a paragraph, because it is the claim that the five questions are one question wearing five masks — but it is not the strongest objection, since the draft's own showcase cases (Milei, welfare nationalism) are genuine counterexamples to equality-monism.

**(b) Converse** is serious but survivable: if only a few percent of citizens deploy even one dimension with constraint, a five-axis-plus-metadata *public* vocabulary misdescribes what mass political language does. The draft's §VIII citation of heuristic left-right inference already lives in Converse's world without saying so. Mitigation: the vocabulary's real users are discourse producers, and elite vocabularies trickle down (as "policy positions" do in the draft's own [^1] account). The draft should state its addressee.

**(c) Poole–Rosenthal** is the objection the draft's own data feed: elite behavior collapses to one or two dimensions, and the draft's CHES composites (.78–.82) show three of its five axes riding one European dimension. The draft's §II disclaimer ("analytically separable, not empirically independent") is the right defense in principle, but as the piece-brief flagged, it verges on unfalsifiable — any correlation pattern confirms it. The strengthening move is to make the framework earn its keep *where the dimensions come apart*: Milei (traditional-ish culture, radically anti-authority economics, insurgent), the welfare nationalists, Sanders-vs-Trump. The cases exist in the draft; they are not currently deployed as answers to a named objection.

**(a) The strongest: Lewis & Lewis's granularity/reification argument.** From the Caplan exchange: the failure of the one-dimensional spectrum is not that one is the wrong number of dimensions but that *bundling itself* is the error — "there is more than one issue in politics"; treat politics like biology and keep issues unbundled ("why not just say 'anti-market' instead of 'left-wing'?"). Applied to the draft: each of the five "questions" is itself a bundle. Economy compresses trade, tax, redistribution, regulation, property, and labor — so a protectionist tax-cutter (Trump) has no true Economy score, only a "3, mixed" that reproduces at axis level exactly the lossy compression the essay denounces at spectrum level. Five axes, on this view, is not decompression but a bigger, better-defended reification — and the tribal dynamics the Lewises document will colonize the new vocabulary the way they colonized the old one. This objection is strongest because it attacks the draft's only unargued load-bearing claim: *why five, and why these five* (the brief's Phase 3 flag, now confirmed as the discourse's likeliest point of attack). **How the draft currently fares: partially armored, by accident.** Its anti-naturalism disclaimer (§II), its "3 can mean five different things" metadata, and its modules-and-tags architecture all tacitly concede granularity; its implicit answer — five is where the marginal named distinction stops paying for its speech cost, i.e., a *pragmatic* optimum between one line and Lewis's issue-atomism — is present in spirit (§VII: "Labels gain explanatory power by excluding detail") but never stated as a reply to anyone. One added section or long paragraph — "Why five and not fifty" — naming the Lewises and Caplan and locating the framework between them would convert the piece's greatest exposure into its sharpest positioning. Without it, the first well-read hostile reviewer writes that section instead.

---

## 4. Misrepresentation check

- **Freeden (§I).** *Accurate as summary.* The draft's gloss — ideologies draw contested concepts from a common field and "give them determinate meaning by placing them into characteristic configurations" — matches the morphological account (core/adjacent/peripheral concepts; decontestation) as corroborated across the Oxford Handbook chapter abstract and secondary summaries. **Flag (tension, not strawman):** Freeden's decontestation thesis holds that pole-words like "liberty" and "equality" have no ideology-independent meaning — yet the draft's coordinate layer requires exactly such stable meanings for its ten poles. The draft borrows Freeden's anti-essentialism for the *names* while quietly exempting its *axes* from morphological relativity. A Freeden-literate reader (the venue's core demographic) can object that the five questions are themselves one more decontestation. Worth a pre-emptive sentence.
- **Mudde (§IV).** *Accurate.* The cited page defines populism as "a thin-centered ideology that considers society to be ultimately separated into two homogenous and antagonistic groups: 'the pure people' and 'the corrupt elite'," politics as expression of the volonté générale. The draft's three-claim unpacking is fair; "homogenous groups" even supports the draft's fourth claim (unitarism). **Flag:** the unitarism/exclusive-representation development is Müller's signature; presenting it as an unattributed "fourth claim [that] often follows" under a Mudde citation shortchanges Müller.
- **Caramani (§IV).** *Accurate, slightly softened.* Abstract: both forms hold "a unitary, nonpluralist, unmediated, and unaccountable vision of society's general interest"; will vs reason. The draft says "relatively unaccountable" — a hedge in Caramani's favor, not against him.
- **Party-families literature (§I).** The draft's characterization (classifiable by origin, organization, affiliation, name, policy, ideology; boundaries don't coincide; expert surveys warn of multi-family membership) is consistent with the standard content of Mair & Mudde 1998, but I did not fetch that article this session — verification belongs to Phase 1's citation check. No red flag on its face.
- **Cosmopolitan–communitarian literature (§III.4).** *Terminology accurate* (confirmed against the cited de Wilde et al. abstract). **Flag (mild):** the cited article's own finding is that the cleavage "lacks a solidified normative component" even in the UK — the draft cites it only for the label, which is defensible, but the article slightly undercuts the axis's crystallization; the broader *Struggle Over Borders* program would be the sturdier anchor.
- **Uscinski et al. (§III.5).** *Accurate* — the abstract confirms a cross-cutting anti-establishment dimension. **Flag (mild):** their dimension carries conspiracist/antisocial freight the draft's charitable Insurgent pole strips away; the draft's normative reconstruction should not be attributed to this source.
- **"The left-right spectrum" as its defenders hold it (§VIII).** *Partial.* The draft fairly represents the heuristic/coordination defense (matching Caplan and its own [^1]). It does **not** represent the substantive defense — Bobbio's equality thesis, Gonzalez's egalitarianism-vs-other-values — and by treating "coalition name" as the only live account of left/right, it quietly wins by definition a debate that is still open. This is the closest thing to a strawman-by-omission in the piece.
- **8values et al.** — no characterization to check: the draft never mentions them. The omission itself is the finding.

---

## 5. Reception forecast

**Venue reality.** [sjsebastian.substack.com](https://sjsebastian.substack.com/archive) is a young, small Substack whose seven essays are all AI-and-philosophy ("What the Model Cannot Give Itself," "The Narcissistic Injury of Artificial Intelligence," "After Bureaucracy"), Bourdieu-inflected, continuous-prose. This piece would be its first politics essay: no primed audience for the topic, and a sharp formal break (tables, notation, a 14-entry bulleted lexicon). In the July-2026 Substack environment — where readers of an AI-focused publication are primed to sniff for machine-made prose — the apparatus-heavy format is the single largest reception risk: numbered axes, scale tables, and symmetrical two-column pole definitions are exactly the surface features hostile readers now pattern-match to "AI-written taxonomy." The mitigation is formal, not just citational: more continuous argumentative prose, fewer tables, and visible authorial stakes.

**Who engages.** (1) *Rationalist-adjacent readers* — likeliest sharers and likeliest source of the deadliest one-liner: "this is 8values with a populism axis and no test." Some will engage generously (this community rewards explicit frameworks and rules of use); the no-master-score rule and the three-layer Trump/Obama/Milei/Orbán sentences are built for them. (2) *Political scientists* — will spot GAL/TAN, welfare chauvinism, Akkerman/Müller, and the informality of the CHES composites (unspecified variable choices; irreproducible as described); a few will appreciate the rules-of-use section as better hygiene than most punditry. (3) *Partisan readers contesting the profiles* — the single most quotable-against-the-author phrase in the draft is Trump as "**market-leaning**" (§VII) in a tariff-and-industrial-policy era; expect it screenshot-quoted without the surrounding apparatus. Milei "culturally traditional in important respects" and the Trump–Meloni–Bolsonaro–**Modi** natcon grouping (Hindu-nationalist specificity; Modi as "natcon" reads as category-flattening to South Asia specialists) are the other two flashpoints. Orbán-as-welfare-nationalist is comparatively safe and genuinely illuminating.

**What gets quoted (favorably):** "The left–right spectrum is not false. It is a compression"; "Left and right are coalition names. The five questions are explanatory coordinates"; "never compute a master score"; the §XII sentence rewrites.

**Pattern-matches to preempt:** "Political Compass with extra steps" (preempt with a one-paragraph genealogy: Nolan → Compass → 8values → 9Axes, and why a *test* is the wrong form — tests score people, this vocabulary describes claims); "8values plagiarism" (name it, credit it, differentiate); "AI-written taxonomy" (form-level fixes); "just rediscovered GAL/TAN" (cite it and make the decomposition argument explicit); "reinvented welfare chauvinism" (one clause).

**Strongest hostile-but-fair reading:** "An elegantly written usage manual for axes that already exist on a quiz site, which never argues why five is the right number, whose own data show three of its five axes are one axis in Europe, and whose best ideas — coalition names above coordinates — were published by Lewis & Lewis in 2023 without the coordinate apparatus." Every clause of that sentence is currently unanswered in the text, and every clause is answerable: the two-function separation and the rules of use are genuinely new; the CHES bundling has a Kitschelt-shaped answer; "why five" has a pragmatic-optimum answer; and the Lewises' eliminativism is precisely what the framework improves on.

**Likeliest misreadings to preempt in the text:** (1) that the five axes are claimed as natural kinds — §II disclaims this, but readers who skim to the lexicon will miss it; a one-line reminder inside §III or §VI would help; (2) that the piece is a centrist both-sides project — the §XI.7 charitable-poles table will be read by some as false moral equivalence (equating fear of "inherited domination" with fear of "dissolution"); the existing disclaimer sentence ("not an assertion that every application is morally equal") carries too much weight for its size; (3) that coordinates are for scoring *people* — quiz-culture readers will ask "what's my number," inverting the piece's classify-arguments-not-identities rule; (4) that Insurgent = populist = bad — §IV's three-way distinction is the antidote but arrives late and dense.
